newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives plan reforms after poll rout.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives plan reforms after poll rout.

text.p: William Hague, the new leader of Britain's shattered Conservatives, on Wednesday spelled out plans to make his party more democratic and prevent it being "outgunned" by the new Labour government.

"Our current organisation is not up to the job. No change is not an option," Hague, elected to replace John Major after the Conservatives' worst-ever electoral trouncing on May 1, told a meeting of members of parliament and local activists.
The Conservatives, who had been in power since 1979, lost half their MPs at the May election, reducing the party's strength to just a quarter of the 659 seats in the House of Commons.

But Hague said the signs of decay had been apparent well before the election. The party had barely a handful of councillors in major cities while party membership, which stood at one million in 1979, had fallen to "a few hundred thousand".

"We can adapt our organisation and campaigning style to the modern age, or we can resign ourselves to being outclassed and outgunned by our Labour and Liberal Democrat opponents," he told the meeting at party headquarters in London.
Hague, elected leader by the party's 164 MPs, promised to follow Britain's other main parties in giving ordinary party members a vote in the election of the party leader.
He will put his own leadership, and his reform plan, to a members' referendum in September.
Other reforms he promised included declaring the identity of all large donors to party funds, and stopping the acceptance of money from rich foreigners.
Major resisted calls to divulge how the party was financed despite allegations that rich businessmen were winning influence over government policy by reaching for their wallets.
The party was dogged in the last parliament by accusations of sleaze, with some MPs admitting taking money to ask parliamentary questions for businessmen.

"We will not tolerate individuals, be they Members of Parliament, councillors or anyone else, who through gross misconduct bring scorn upon the whole of our Party. In exceptional circumstances, the Party needs powers either to suspend or expel," Hague said.
He expressed optimism that the changes, coupled with a thorough policy review, could return the party to power at the next election, due in 2002.

But the Conservatives' road back to power may have become even more stony following an agreement on Tuesday between Blair and the Liberal Democrats, who almost doubled their parliamentary representation to 46 seats in May.

Blair offered the Liberals places on a consultative cabinet committee which will look into constitutional reform. Aides said the move was in part an attempt to ensure Blair could secure Liberal support in parliament if he ever needed it.
At a meeting of Labour MPs on Wednesday, Blair stressed his ambition to become the first Labour Prime Minister to hold power for two full parliamentary terms, or around 10 years.
"Our task must be to govern for the long term so that when the next election comes, the people of this country trust us and want to re-elect us with a continuing mandate," Blair said.
